blocks.text: In Arabic this same animal is called اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, and the lexicographers who render it as talpa [mole] are mistaken. The matter will become clear from the description. Damir, in the chapter On اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, says: هو حيوان طويل الرجلين وقصير اليدين جدا [huwa ḥayawān ṭawīl al-rijlayn wa-qaṣīr al-yadayn jiddan] It is an animal whose hind feet are long and whose fore feet are very short. And a little later: فهي قصيرة اليدين لانها اذا خافت شي لاذت بالصعود فلا يلحقها شي [fa-hiya qaṣīrat al-yadayn li-annahā idhā khāfat shay lādhat bi-l-ṣuʿūd fa-lā yalḥaquhā shay] And it has short fore feet so that, when it fears something, it may flee upward, and no animal can overtake it. And further on: قال الجاحظ والقزويني وهو من نوع الفار [qāla al-Jāḥiẓ wa-l-Qazwīnī wa-huwa min nawʿ al-fār] Algiahid and Alkazuinius have said that it is among the species of mouse. [col. 1011] It is therefore truly an ἀρκτομῦς [arktomys], that is, a mouse that has this in common with the bear, that it walks on its hind feet, which are the longer. Gesner, in the chapter On the Alpine mouse, cites an anonymous Greek writer, not yet published, who in a little book On animals has the following about the arctomys: One arctomys keeps watch while the others feed, and each of them brings it a share of the fodder. But if it has been too careless in its watch, and some man has come upon them whose approach it did not betray with its voice, it is killed by the others. See how very similar to this is what Damir says of the aljarbuo, so that you may know that it is the same animal! هو من الحيوان الذي له رييس مطاع يناقده [huwa min al-ḥayawān alladhī lahu raʾīs muṭāʿ yunāqiduhu] [II, 422] اليه واذا كان فيها يكون بيتها في مكان مشرف او علي صخرة ينظر الي الطريق من كل ناحية فان راي ما يخافه صر باسنانه وصوت فاذا سمعته انصرفت الي حجرتها فان قصر الرييس حتي ادركهم احد وصاد منهم شيا اجتمعوا علي الرييس وقتلوا وولوا غيره [ilayhi wa-idhā kāna fīhā yakūn baytuhā fī makān mushrif aw ʿalā ṣakhra yanẓuru ilā al-ṭarīq min kull nāḥiya fa-in raʾā mā yakhāfuhu ṣarra bi-asnānihi wa-ṣawwata fa-idhā samiʿathu inṣarafat ilā ḥujratihā fa-in qaṣṣara al-raʾīs ḥattā adrakahum aḥad wa-ṣāda minhum shayʾan ijtamaʿū ʿalā al-raʾīs wa-qatalū wa-wallaw ghayrahu] That mouse is one of the animals that have a leader whom they honour and obey. When it is among those whose dwelling is in a high place or on a rock, it looks out from there over the path in every direction. And if it sees anything to be feared, it gnashes its teeth and cries out; on hearing this, they withdraw to their hiding-places. But if it holds back until someone overtakes them, or catches one of their number, they conspire against the leader, kill it, and put another in its place. If you want more about the same animal, hear the rest of Damir: ويسمى الدرص وذو الرمح ورمحه ذنبه وله ذنب كذنب الجرد يرفعه صعدا في طرفه شبه النوارة ولونه كلون الغزال [wa-yusammā al-dirṣ wa-dhū al-rumḥ wa-rumḥuhu dhanabuhu wa-lahu dhanab ka-dhanab al-jurd yarfaʿuhu ṣuʿudan fī ṭarafihi shibh al-nawwāra wa-lawnuhu ka-lawn al-ghazāl] It is also called dirs and dur-romchi (that is, the spear-bearer); for in place of a spear it has a tail, like the tail of a mouse, which it raises upward; and at its tip there is something like a flower ^{(8)}. Its colour is like the colour of the gazelle, or roe-deer ^{(9)}. There follows: وهذا الحيوان يسكن بطن الارض ليقوم رطوبتها له مقام الما [wa-hādhā al-ḥayawān yaskun baṭn al-arḍ li-yaqūm ruṭūbatuhā lahu maqām al-mā] This animal lives in the belly of the earth, so that its moisture may serve it in place of water. And a little further on: واليربوع يتخذ حجره في نشر من الارض ثم يحفر بيته في مهب والرياح الاربع ويتخذ [wa-l-yarbūʿ yattakhidhu juḥrahu fī nashr min al-arḍ thumma yaḥfiru baytahu fī mahabb wa-l-riyāḥ al-arbaʿ wa-yattakhidhu] [col. 1012] فيه كوي وتسمي النافقا والقاصعا والراهطا فاذا طلب من احدي هذه الكوي نافق اي خرج من النافقا وان طلب من النافقا خرج من القاصعا وان طلب من القاصعا خرج من الراهطا [fīhi kuwā wa-tusammā al-nāfiqā wa-l-qāṣiʿā wa-l-rāhiṭā fa-idhā ṭuliba min iḥdā hādhihi al-kuwā nāfaqa ay kharaja min al-nāfiqā wa-in ṭuliba min al-nāfiqā kharaja min al-qāṣiʿā wa-in ṭuliba min al-qāṣiʿā kharaja min al-rāhiṭā] The aljarbuo prepares its hiding-place by scattering the earth, and digs itself a dwelling open to the blowing of the four winds, and furnishes it with windows [II, 423] one of which is called naphika, another kasia, and rahita. If it is attacked from these, it goes out through the naphika. And if it is attacked from the naphika, it goes out through the kasia; or through the rahita, if from the kasia. Just as Plautus says of our mouse in the Truculentus, act 4:
Consider what a wise beast the tiny mouse is, which never entrusts its life to a single lair: for if one entrance is besieged, it has another refuge ^{b)}.
